content:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Harborview Payments x Redwood Inference — Console demo + eval next steps
Date: Jan 13, 2026
Time: 3:00pm PT
Duration: 47 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Priyom Das (Redwood Inference, AE)
- Fatima Noor (Redwood Inference, Solutions Engineering)
- Maya Chen (Harborview Payments, Director Platform Eng)
- Tom Alvarez (Harborview Payments, Staff ML Eng)
- Renee Patel (Harborview Payments, Security & GRC)
- Eric Jensen (Harborview Payments, Procurement Ops)

Summary (auto-generated)
- Redwood demoed the Redwood Console (usage, latency, errors, and per-route/model breakdown) and discussed deployment options (Hosted, Dedicated, Private/VPC).
- Harborview asked detailed questions on p95 latency, cost per token, rate limiting, and how batching/caching impacts tail latency.
- Security topics included audit logging, retention boundaries, encryption/KMS integration, and data residency.
- Agreement to scope a short evaluation with Redwood providing suggested config and Harborview providing representative payload samples.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Console walkthrough: request tracing, token accounting, dashboards
- Performance: p50/p95, streaming, throughput vs latency tradeoffs
- Cost drivers: prompt caching, continuous batching, model selection
- Deployment: Dedicated vs Private/VPC considerations
- Security/compliance: audit logs, retention, KMS/HSM options, SSO/RBAC
- Evaluation plan + next steps

Action items (auto-generated)
- Harborview to send sample payloads and expected traffic profile.
- Redwood to send security FAQ addendum + retention/residency language.
- Schedule security follow-up and technical sizing.

Transcript

[00:00] Priyom Das: Alright, cool. I think we’re live. Thanks everyone for making time. I have Fatima on from Solutions Engineering. The goal today is a quick console walkthrough and then we can dig into cost and latency questions, and if it makes sense, align on what a scoped evaluation looks like.

[00:18] Maya Chen: Sounds good.

[00:19] Tom Alvarez: Yep.

[00:20] Renee Patel: Hi.

[00:22] Eric Jensen: Hey.

[00:24] Priyom Das: Great. Before we jump in, just to level set—Maya, last time you mentioned you’re currently split between Bedrock for a couple things and some direct OpenAI usage for others, and exploring whether you can standardize inference. Is that still the framing?

[00:39] Maya Chen: Yeah. It’s a bit messy. Different teams picked different providers. The biggest pain is cost predictability and also security reviews every time someone wants to add a new endpoint.

[00:50] Priyom Das: Makes sense. And your use case, Tom, you said primarily like customer support summarization and some compliance-y message review?

[00:58] Tom Alvarez: Right. Summaries, tagging, then we have a “communications review” thing that flags risky language in outbound emails and chat scripts. Not literally trading, but still regulated-ish.

[01:10] Priyom Das: Yup. That’s exactly the pattern we see in payments. Cool. Fatima, want to drive the demo?

[01:15] Fatima Noor: Sure. Let me share my screen.

[01:22] Fatima Noor: Okay—can everyone see the Redwood Console?

[01:24] Maya Chen: Yes.

[01:25] Tom Alvarez: Yep.

[01:26] Fatima Noor: Great. So what I’m showing is a test workspace, but this mirrors what you’d get in Hosted, Dedicated, or Private. Left nav: Usage, Latency, Errors, Models, and then Deployments and Settings.

[01:40] Fatima Noor: Starting in Usage. You can slice by API key, route, model, region. For example, I’m filtering to the “comms-review” route.

[01:51] Fatima Noor: Here’s token volume over time. And then below, cost breakdown. We split prompt tokens, completion tokens, plus any embeddings endpoints separately.

[02:03] Tom Alvarez: When you say cost breakdown, is it like per 1k token unit or actual dollars?

[02:07] Fatima Noor: Both. This view is dollars, but you can switch the unit to cost per 1k tokens or per request. We also expose effective cost after caching/batching so you can see the delta.

[02:19] Maya Chen: That’s useful. One of our issues is we get surprised by long prompts.

[02:24] Fatima Noor: Yeah. In Latency tab, we show distribution and also correlate to input length. Let me click Latency.

[02:31] Fatima Noor: So here: p50, p95, p99. You can select “time-to-first-token” versus “end-to-end”. And streaming changes the story, obviously.

[02:44] Tom Alvarez: We care about time to first token for chat-y things. But for comms review it’s more like total. Do you separate those in the metrics?

[02:51] Fatima Noor: Exactly. TTFT is tracked separately. Also, you can add “queue time” if you’re in Dedicated or Private and want to see when you’re saturating.

[03:04] Maya Chen: So queue time, is that like before it hits the GPU batch?

[03:07] Fatima Noor: Right, it’s basically waiting in the scheduler for a slot. Helps you decide if you need more capacity or tune batching.

[03:15] Priyom Das: And just to connect this: in Dedicated you can get predictable throughput because you’re not sharing the GPU pool with other customers.

[03:22] Renee Patel: Quick question—when you say “other customers” that’s only Hosted, right?

[03:26] Priyom Das: Correct. Hosted is multi-tenant by default with logical isolation. Dedicated is single-tenant GPU pools. Private is your VPC or on-prem.

[03:35] Renee Patel: Okay.

[03:37] Fatima Noor: I’ll show Errors quickly. It’s basic, but it’s helpful: rate limit, upstream errors, timeouts, policy blocks if you use guardrails. You can click an error and see example request IDs.

[03:50] Tom Alvarez: You have tracing? Like per request?

[03:53] Fatima Noor: Yes. Under “Requests” (it’s in this submenu), you can search by request_id or correlation id. Let me open one.

[04:05] Fatima Noor: You’ll see the route, model version, tokens in/out, latency breakdown (queue, prefill, decode), and then—this is optional—prompt/output logging. Most regulated customers disable payload logging and just keep metadata.

[04:22] Renee Patel: Wait, you said prompt logging optional. So by default, do you store prompts and responses?

[04:28] Fatima Noor: In Hosted, default is no long-term storage of raw prompts/outputs for product purposes. There is transient processing to serve the request, and then logs are configurable. Typically customers choose metadata-only logs. If you enable payload logging for debugging, it’s explicit and has a retention window.

[04:46] Renee Patel: Okay. We’ll need exact language. We get asked “do you retain prompts, yes or no” and “how long” and “where.”

[04:54] Priyom Das: Totally. We have a FinServ security FAQ addendum we can share that has questionnaire-ready wording. We can also schedule a short follow-up with our security team if helpful.

[05:03] Renee Patel: Great.

[05:05] Fatima Noor: Also, in Private, those logs are under your control entirely—ship to your SIEM, your storage, your retention.

[05:12] Maya Chen: Okay. Let’s talk performance. Our current pain is tail latency. We can hit p50 okay, but p95 blows up during peak. We think it’s capacity contention and sometimes provider throttles.

[05:25] Fatima Noor: Yeah, that’s common. Two knobs: capacity and concurrency management, and then batching/caching behavior. With our scheduler we do continuous batching. You can cap max batch size to protect p95, or allow bigger batches for cost.

[05:40] Tom Alvarez: How does caching work? Like prefix caching? KV cache?

[05:43] Fatima Noor: Right, prefix caching for repeated system prompts / templates. We also have KV cache management to reuse the prefix compute. The win is big if you have standardized prompts, which comms review often does.

[05:57] Tom Alvarez: But does that increase memory and reduce throughput?

[06:00] Fatima Noor: It uses GPU memory, yes, but net it often improves throughput because you avoid recomputing the prefix. We’d benchmark with your token distribution.

[06:11] Maya Chen: We’re also worried about noisy neighbor if we stick in Hosted.

[06:15] Priyom Das: That’s where Dedicated comes in. Usually the pattern is Hosted for initial testing, then Dedicated when you want predictable SLOs and isolation. And for strict data boundary, Private/VPC.

[06:26] Eric Jensen: From procurement side, what triggers the move? Like do we sign different agreements?

[06:31] Priyom Das: Hosted is usage-based; Dedicated is reserved capacity contract. Private is enterprise license + support and usually a separate security addendum. We can keep it simple for eval—typically start on Hosted or a small Dedicated slice depending on requirements.

[06:47] Renee Patel: If any production traffic includes cardholder data, we usually don’t allow multi-tenant unless there’s a strong story. We’re not full PCI scope for everything, but we’re conservative.

[06:58] Priyom Das: Understood. A lot of payment processors we talk to go to Dedicated or Private for that reason. We can map your data classification to the right deployment.

[07:08] Fatima Noor: On the latency side: for Dedicated, you can see queue time in the console and set alerts. You can also set autoscaling policies if you have bursty load.

[07:18] Maya Chen: For dedicated, is autoscaling like adding GPUs automatically? Or is that manual?

[07:22] Fatima Noor: It’s policy-based within your reserved pool plus optional burst capacity, depending on what you contract. For strict predictable cost, you can keep it fixed.

[07:33] Tom Alvarez: Can you talk about expected latencies? Like, say we’re doing a 2k prompt and 300 token completion. We need p95 under, I don’t know, 2.5 seconds for comms review.

[07:45] Fatima Noor: It depends on model choice and hardware, but that’s within the realm. For example, a 7B–13B class model with optimized kernels can hit that; for larger models it’s tighter. Another approach is using a smaller model for classification and only fall back to a bigger model on ambiguous cases.

[08:04] Tom Alvarez: So routing.

[08:05] Fatima Noor: Exactly. Smart routing and fallback is supported. You can set policies by route.

[08:13] Maya Chen: What about function calling / tool calling? We’re not heavy into it, but it’s on the roadmap.

[08:18] Fatima Noor: Supported. We also support structured outputs. But for your current workload, the big wins are stability and cost.

[08:28] Priyom Das: Maybe we double click on cost since it’s a big motivator for you.

[08:32] Maya Chen: Yeah. We need to be able to explain to finance why it’s not going to spike. Also, we’re trying to get to a consistent “cost per review” number.

[08:43] Priyom Das: Right. In console, you can attribute cost by route, and then divide by “reviews processed” if you send a custom metric or just count requests.

[08:54] Tom Alvarez: Do you have anything like a “cost per 1k tokens” you guarantee? Or is it best effort?

[08:59] Priyom Das: Pricing is per token, so cost is deterministic given tokens. The variability comes from how many tokens your prompts generate, and any retries/timeouts, and whether you stream. For Dedicated, you can also think in terms of cost per throughput because you pay for capacity.

[09:16] Eric Jensen: Dedicated sounds like it could be easier for budgeting.

[09:18] Priyom Das: Exactly. Some teams prefer that. Hosted is great for early stage and variable workloads.

[09:26] Maya Chen: On latency, do you provide an SLA? Like p95.

[09:31] Priyom Das: For enterprise tiers, yes, we can commit to uptime and some latency targets depending on deployment and workload definition. Usually we define it as region + model + max input length.

[09:44] Renee Patel: I’m going to ask the security stuff now so we don’t forget. For audit logs—do we get admin activity logs? Like who created keys, who changed routing rules?

[09:53] Fatima Noor: Yes, we have audit logs for control-plane actions: API key creation, role changes, deployment changes, routing policy updates. In Hosted and Dedicated we can export those logs; in Private you can push them to your SIEM directly.

[10:10] Renee Patel: Export formats? We typically use Splunk. JSON, syslog, whatever.

[10:14] Fatima Noor: JSON log export; integrations vary by deployment. We can do S3-based export and then you ingest into Splunk, or direct HTTP collector in some setups. We’d confirm what’s supported in your preferred mode.

[10:28] Renee Patel: Okay. And encryption—at rest and in transit, obvious, but do you support customer managed keys?

[10:35] Fatima Noor: For Private, yes—KMS integration point so you can control key material. For Hosted/Dedicated, we have options, but it depends on region and the exact key management requirements. We should align on what you mean by “customer managed”—like BYOK versus envelope encryption.

[10:52] Renee Patel: We’ll need that clarification.

[10:54] Priyom Das: We can loop in our security engineering lead if needed. But for eval, we can start with the standard posture and then map requirements.

[11:04] Tom Alvarez: Another question. We’ve experimented with vLLM in-house. It’s fast for some stuff, but we spend a lot of time tuning and we don’t have good observability. How do you compare to just running vLLM ourselves?

[11:18] Fatima Noor: vLLM is great. The delta is: operational tooling, multi-model rollouts, tracing, per-route policies, and managed upgrades. Also some runtime features like smarter batching and cache handling plus consistent instrumentation. If you have a platform team that wants to own everything, self-host can work, but the hidden cost is reliability and on-call.

[11:41] Maya Chen: That’s basically our situation. We don’t want another thing to babysit.

[11:45] Priyom Das: Exactly. And the “Hosted → Dedicated → Private” path is designed so you can start quickly and not rewrite your app.

[11:55] Maya Chen: Can you show me the model versioning and rollback piece? We had one incident where a model upgrade changed outputs and we had to scramble.

[12:03] Fatima Noor: Yup. Under Models, you can pin versions per route. Here, “comms-review” is pinned to model X version 1.2.3. If you want to test a new version, you create a canary, route 5% traffic, compare metrics, then promote or rollback.

[12:22] Tom Alvarez: Do you have evals built in? Like golden set?

[12:26] Fatima Noor: We have hooks for that, and some customers integrate their own eval harness. Redwood Optimize can alert on regressions if you connect prompt sets.

[12:37] Maya Chen: Okay.

[12:39] Eric Jensen: Sorry, I’m jumping around, but contract-wise—if we do a short evaluation, what’s the typical duration?

[12:46] Priyom Das: Usually 2–3 weeks for a technical eval. Sometimes longer if security review is heavy. The goal is: confirm latency/cost at your expected traffic, and confirm deployment/security posture.

[12:59] Eric Jensen: And do you charge for that?

[13:01] Priyom Das: Depends. Often we do credits for Hosted, or a small paid pilot for Dedicated. We can propose something after we see scope.

[13:10] Maya Chen: We’d rather do something structured. We’ve wasted time on “free” evals that don’t answer anything.

[13:16] Priyom Das: Love that. We’ll keep it tight.

[13:19] Fatima Noor: To scope it, we need: expected QPS, concurrency, prompt/completion token distribution, region, and any hard constraints like “must be in VPC.”

[13:32] Maya Chen: We can provide traffic patterns. Peak is about… for comms review, maybe 80 requests per second at peak, but bursts to 150 when batch jobs run.

[13:41] Tom Alvarez: Concurrency is high because our system fans out.

[13:45] Fatima Noor: Okay. That’s meaningful. In Hosted, you might hit rate limits; Dedicated would smooth it out.

[13:53] Tom Alvarez: Are rate limits configurable? We got throttled pretty hard on one provider.

[13:58] Priyom Das: We can set quotas per key/route. In Hosted, there are default tier limits; in enterprise we can raise them. In Dedicated, you essentially own the capacity.

[14:10] Renee Patel: Data residency: we need US-only. Preferably West or Central.

[14:15] Priyom Das: We can do US regions. If you need specific residency guarantees, that’s usually easier in Dedicated/Private.

[14:24] Maya Chen: What about VPC connectivity? We can’t send traffic over public internet from some systems.

[14:30] Fatima Noor: For Private in your VPC, that’s straightforward—private endpoints, security groups, you control routing. For Dedicated, we can also support private connectivity patterns depending on cloud. We’d go through networking assumptions in a technical deep dive.

[14:47] Tom Alvarez: Today, our app runs in AWS. We can do VPC peering, PrivateLink, etc.

[14:52] Fatima Noor: Great—PrivateLink is commonly used.

[14:56] Priyom Das: This is probably a good point to ask: is Private a hard requirement for your eval, or can we start on Hosted to benchmark quickly?

[15:05] Maya Chen: For benchmarking, Hosted is okay as long as we don’t send anything sensitive. We can use synthetic data.

[15:12] Renee Patel: Yeah, synthetic or heavily redacted only. No real customer data.

[15:17] Priyom Das: Perfect.

[15:18] Fatima Noor: Then we can run an initial benchmark on Hosted and use that to size Dedicated or Private.

[15:26] Tom Alvarez: Okay. But we need realistic token lengths. We can generate fake messages similar length.

[15:32] Fatima Noor: Right. If you can send 2–3 representative payload templates (minus sensitive content), that helps.

[15:42] Priyom Das: Also you asked earlier about “cost per review.” We can instrument your route so you get cost per request and then you can roll that up.

[15:51] Maya Chen: Does the console let me export usage data? We have our own BI.

[15:56] Fatima Noor: Yes, exports via API; and scheduled reports in some tiers.

[16:03] Maya Chen: Good.

[16:05] Tom Alvarez: Another technical question: do you support embeddings and reranking? We may want a search component later.

[16:11] Priyom Das: Yes. Same API surface.

[16:14] Fatima Noor: And those show up in the same usage/latency dashboards.

[16:19] Renee Patel: SSO and RBAC—do you have SAML? We can’t have shared admin accounts.

[16:25] Priyom Das: Yes, SSO/SAML for enterprise; RBAC roles for console access. Again, we’ll share exact details in the security addendum.

[16:35] Renee Patel: Great.

[16:37] Eric Jensen: If we do the eval and it goes well, what’s the typical timeline to contract? I’m trying to plan.

[16:44] Priyom Das: If security review is straightforward, 4–6 weeks isn’t unusual. If you need Private deployment and heavy legal, sometimes 8–12. But we can parallelize: start the technical eval while Renee starts security questionnaire.

[16:59] Renee Patel: If you can send the SOC2 report under NDA, that helps.

[17:03] Priyom Das: Yes, we can do that under NDA.

[17:05] Fatima Noor: And we can provide an architecture doc for Private/VPC to speed up the review.

[17:10] Maya Chen: That would be great.

[17:12] Tom Alvarez: Can you show how you’d do a fallback model? Like if the main model errors.

[17:17] Fatima Noor: Sure. In Routing Policies, you can define primary and fallback. Example: primary model A in us-west, fallback model B in us-west, and if capacity constrained, optionally fallback to us-central. You can set conditions: error rate threshold, latency threshold.

[17:38] Tom Alvarez: Okay, that’s exactly what we need. We had a couple provider incidents where we got 429s and had no automatic fallback.

[17:46] Priyom Das: Right, and we can set that so your app doesn’t need to implement provider-specific logic.

[17:52] Maya Chen: So in your experience, for payments use cases, do people go Dedicated or Private?

[17:59] Priyom Das: It varies. If it’s mostly non-sensitive text and the goal is just performance/cost, Dedicated is common. If it touches higher regulated data or you have strict network boundary requirements, Private in VPC. Some start Dedicated and later move to Private.

[18:16] Renee Patel: The network boundary might be the deciding factor.

[18:19] Maya Chen: Also, we need consistent audit logging.

[18:22] Fatima Noor: Both Dedicated and Private can do audit logs, but Private gives you the most control.

[18:28] Tom Alvarez: How hard is it to migrate? Like if we start on Hosted.

[18:31] Fatima Noor: Same API. Mostly endpoint/base URL and credentials. If you use special networking like PrivateLink, that’s additional config. But app-level changes should be minimal.

[18:44] Priyom Das: That’s the intent of the platform.

[18:47] Maya Chen: Okay. Can we talk numbers? Not pricing exactly, but what do you need from us to estimate Dedicated sizing.

[18:55] Fatima Noor: We need peak QPS, average QPS, concurrency, token lengths, and target p95. Also whether you need streaming. Then we can propose a GPU type and count. And we can validate in the eval.

[19:12] Tom Alvarez: Our p95 target is 2.5 sec for comms review and maybe 1.2 sec time-to-first-token for chat assist.

[19:20] Fatima Noor: Great, two distinct routes, different SLOs. We can separate configs.

[19:28] Priyom Das: And from commercial side, we can package that as a small Dedicated pool with burst or not.

[19:35] Eric Jensen: Helpful.

[19:36] Renee Patel: One more security question: do you do data deletion? If we accidentally send something.

[19:43] Fatima Noor: There are controls. If payload logging is off, there’s nothing retained beyond transient processing. For retained logs, we can delete based on retention policies. For Private, you own the storage and deletion.

[19:57] Renee Patel: Okay. We’ll want that in writing.

[20:00] Priyom Das: Yep.

[20:02] Maya Chen: Fatima, can you show me how you’d detect a latency regression? Like after changing batching.

[20:08] Fatima Noor: Sure. In Latency tab, you can overlay changes. There’s an annotation when a deployment policy changes. For example, here’s a “config update” event. Then you can compare p95 before/after.

[20:25] Tom Alvarez: That’s nice.

[20:27] Fatima Noor: And you can drill down to request traces to see if regression is from queue time or decode time.

[20:35] Maya Chen: Okay.

[20:37] Priyom Das: I want to make sure we capture your questions on model providers. You’re using OpenAI and Bedrock today. Any Anthropic?

[20:44] Tom Alvarez: We tested Claude for summarization but it was expensive and also the data story was complicated.

[20:50] Priyom Das: Got it.

[20:52] Maya Chen: We don’t want to manage five providers. We want one inference layer and the ability to move later.

[20:58] Priyom Das: That’s exactly our pitch.

[21:01] Eric Jensen: Are the models you run all open models? Or do you broker closed models?

[21:06] Priyom Das: Mostly curated open models and Redwood-verified profiles. The advantage is deployment flexibility, including Private. For some customers, that’s key.

[21:17] Tom Alvarez: We’re okay with open models if quality is good enough.

[21:20] Fatima Noor: In the eval we can test a couple options. Usually comms review can do well with smaller models if prompt is well designed.

[21:31] Maya Chen: Cool.

[21:33] Priyom Das: Let’s align on evaluation scope. What would be the “yes/no” by end of eval?

[21:39] Maya Chen: For me: can you meet our latency under load, and can you give us predictable cost. And can security sign off enough to proceed.

[21:50] Tom Alvarez: For me: output quality stable, and the routing/fallback works.

[21:55] Renee Patel: For me: clear retention boundaries, audit logging, SSO, and a path to VPC deployment.

[22:02] Eric Jensen: For me: a clear commercial proposal that’s not going to change three times.

[22:08] Priyom Das: All fair.

[22:10] Fatima Noor: For the eval, we can define two routes: comms review (non-streaming) and agent assist (streaming). We’ll pick one model each, measure p50/p95, and cost per request. Then we can do a second pass with caching/batching tuned.

[22:30] Tom Alvarez: We can do that.

[22:32] Maya Chen: How quickly can we start?

[22:35] Priyom Das: As soon as you send sample payload shapes and we provision a workspace. We can do that today.

[22:42] Maya Chen: Okay.

[22:43] Renee Patel: And you’ll send the security docs.

[22:45] Priyom Das: Yes.

[22:47] Fatima Noor: Also, if you have strict egress allowlisting, Hosted will be public endpoints, so just keep it synthetic for now.

[22:56] Maya Chen: Yep.

[22:58] Tom Alvarez: When you say sample payloads, do you need actual text?

[23:01] Fatima Noor: Not necessarily. Token length matters, so you can use lorem ipsum-like content as long as it’s similar length and structure. Also include the system prompt template.

[23:15] Tom Alvarez: Got it.

[23:16] Priyom Das: We can send you a template for what to provide.

[23:20] Maya Chen: Okay.

[23:22] Eric Jensen: Can I ask—if this goes Private/VPC, who operates what? Like do we have to run Kubernetes?

[23:30] Fatima Noor: Private can be packaged. In many cases, Redwood provides the control plane and runtime components; there are options depending on environment. Some customers run on their EKS, some use managed. We’d do an architecture session with Simran (our reference architect) if you want to go deep.

[23:51] Maya Chen: We’d like that. We have an internal platform, but we don’t want to own every detail.

[23:57] Priyom Das: Let’s do a separate technical deep dive on Private deployment architecture.

[24:01] Maya Chen: Yes.

[24:03] Renee Patel: I’d join.

[24:05] Priyom Das: Perfect.

[24:07] Fatima Noor: One more thing: if we do Dedicated first, it’s a good stepping stone. But since you have VPC constraints, we should validate what’s acceptable.

[24:18] Maya Chen: Agreed.

[24:20] Tom Alvarez: Are you able to do request-level metadata export without content? Like token counts, latency, model.

[24:26] Fatima Noor: Yes. That’s the default for regulated. Request_id, timestamps, tokens, latencies, status codes, route, model version.

[24:38] Tom Alvarez: Great.

[24:40] Priyom Das: Any other questions we haven’t covered?

[24:44] Maya Chen: I think we’re good.

[24:46] Renee Patel: I’ll want to see that exact retention wording.

[24:50] Priyom Das: Yep.

[24:51] Eric Jensen: And I’ll want a sense of Dedicated pricing bands when you have sizing.

[24:56] Priyom Das: Understood.

[25:00] Priyom Das: Let me recap next steps so we’re aligned.

[25:03] Priyom Das: One: Tom/Maya, you’ll send us 2–3 representative payload templates, token length expectations, and rough traffic profile—peak QPS and concurrency. Two: Fatima will propose an eval plan with the models and config and success criteria. Three: I’ll send the security FAQ addendum and we’ll schedule a 30-minute security follow-up with Renee. Four: we’ll book a 60-minute technical sizing and Private/VPC architecture session.

[25:33] Maya Chen: Works.

[25:34] Tom Alvarez: Yep.

[25:35] Renee Patel: Works.

[25:36] Eric Jensen: Fine by me.

[25:38] Priyom Das: Awesome. Anything else before we drop?

[25:41] Fatima Noor: All good.

[25:42] Maya Chen: Thanks.

[25:43] Priyom Das: Thanks everyone.

[25:45] Meeting ended

Note: Transcript generated by Fireflies.ai. Minor transcription errors may be present.
